why: If the base's errors come from degrading over its own long context, answer length separates wrong from right answers strongly, beyond the cap hits alone.
Restarting long answers gives a fresh attempt on the same long problem, where the base degrades again, so it recovers only a few of the 77 cap-hit problems.
Failures on the 328 are systematic on long problems (the base degrades on every sample), so a 4-sample vote adds only a few points over 164.
The base fails the long-solution problems on nearly every sample, so pass@4 stays near RL's single-sample 206 instead of climbing well above it.
T 1.0 helps the base only by escaping repetition attractors in its own long context; min-p 0.1 cuts the tail and brings part of the looping back, so accuracy falls below 410.
Top-p 0.95 truncation at T 1.0 brings back part of the low-temperature looping (as at T 0.6, where top-p 0.95 cost 24 problems), so accuracy falls below 410.
Truncating the sampling tail at T 1.0 brings back some rule-A loops (0 at plain T 1.0, 71 at T 0.6).
Min-p truncation restores some repetition attractors and drift, so cap hits rise above the 27 at plain T 1.0.
The RL change depends on long math context and grows with position, so one constant vector per layer closes little of the KL.
On RL's own long text the change is context-dependent and grows with position, so a constant per-layer vector closes little of the KL.
A constant vector on the MLP output alone captures even less of a context-dependent change.
A constant vector on the MLP output alone captures even less of a context-dependent change on RL text.
The base's remaining errors cluster on long problems where it degrades on every sample, so a 4-sample vote adds about 10 over 410.
At T 1.0 the 27 cap hits are drift on long problems, not loops, so restarts recover only a few of them (unlike T 0.6, where restarts recovered loops).
Long-solution problems fail on nearly every base sample, so pass@4 stays below RL's 463 single sample.
